section_title: Why does Jesus call John more than a prophet?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 24 After John’s messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? 25 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces. 26 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. 27 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’ 28 I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

29 All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice. For they had received the baptism of John. 30 But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John.

context_lines: After John’s messengers leave, Jesus speaks to the crowd about John himself. His questions set the wilderness messenger apart from a reed that bends with the wind and from someone living in palace luxury. He directs attention to John’s prophetic calling.

John is more than a prophet because he is the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way. Jesus then gives John extraordinary praise while saying that even the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he. The statement draws attention to the significance of the kingdom John has announced.

The passage closes with contrasting responses. People who had received John’s baptism, including tax collectors, acknowledge God’s justice. The Pharisees and experts in the law described here had refused that baptism and rejected God’s purpose for themselves. Their response to John’s call is part of their response to the work Jesus is now making known.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly recognize John as the promised forerunner whose importance comes from preparing the way for Jesus. The comparison with the least in the kingdom receives different explanations.

The Catholic bishops’ note on the parallel Matthew passage emphasizes the great privilege of belonging to the kingdom John announced. Wesley takes the least here more specifically as the least teacher Jesus sends out. These are explanations of the comparison in a set of notes and a commentator’s work; they do not mean John is simply being dismissed as unfaithful. ([USCCB note on Matthew 11:11](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/matthew/11); [Wesley on Luke 7:28](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/))
god_plan_lines: Jesus explicitly identifies John with the messenger promised in Scripture. Malachi describes a messenger preparing the way before the Lord’s coming; Jesus applies that preparing role to John. This places their ministries within the promised approach of God to His people. ([Malachi 3:1](https://biblehub.com/bsb/malachi/3.htm); [Luke 7:27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/7.htm))

John’s own testimony in the fourth Gospel gives a related picture. He is sent ahead of the Christ and rejoices as the bridegroom’s friend when the bridegroom arrives. The point of his ministry is to direct people toward Jesus, and his joy is bound up with Jesus becoming greater. ([John 3:25–30](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/3.htm))
